vt8_jesuits.topic: Society of Jesus: founding, fourth vow, suppression and restoration, size, Francis, what it controls

claims.text: On 15 August 1534 Ignatius of Loyola and six companions (Xavier, Salmerón, Laínez, Bobadilla, Faber, Rodrigues) took vows at Montmartre; Paul III confirmed the order on 27 September 1540 and Ignatius was chosen first Superior General; the Society is the largest Catholic male religious order, with its curia in Rome.

Regimini militantis Ecclesiae (27 September 1540, Paul III) approved the Society, capped it at 60 members, and its Formula of the Institute required Jesuits to accept missions from the pope through their superior; Julius III's Exposcit debitum (21 July 1550) gave final approval and removed the cap.

The fourth vow of professed Jesuits is a vow of obedience to the pope concerning missions, i.e. to go where the pope sends them; after final vows the professed also take simple vows not to seek church dignities such as becoming a bishop, nor high office in the Society, and to report anyone who does.

Expulsions: Portugal 1759, France 1764, Spain and Naples 1767, Parma 1768; Clement XIV suppressed the Society by Dominus ac Redemptor, 21 July 1773 ('we abolish and suppress'); Catherine II in Russia and Frederick II in Prussia refused to promulgate it.
Pius VII restored the Society by the bull Sollicitudo omnium ecclesiarum, 7 August 1814.
Society's own count at 1 January 2022: 14,439 Jesuits (10,432 priests, 2,587 scholastics, 837 brothers, 583 novices).

Jorge Mario Bergoglio entered the Jesuit novitiate on 11 March 1958, was ordained on 13 December 1969, became provincial of Argentina in 1973, bishop in 1992, cardinal on 21 February 2001, and was elected pope on 13 March 2013.
USCCB: on 13 March 2013 Francis became 'the first pope from the Americas, the first Jesuit, the 266th pope'.
As of 16 October 2026, Arturo Sosa Abascal, the 31st Superior General, elected 14 October 2016, was visiting Ghana; the report mentions no upcoming General Congregation.

After Arrupe's stroke on 7 August 1981, John Paul II disregarded Arrupe's request to appoint Vincent O'Keefe and appointed Paolo Dezza and Giuseppe Pittau as interim leaders; GC33 to elect a successor was allowed only after two years (1983, Kolvenbach).
Jesuit education 2024: 177 universities in the IAJU; 937 schools in the Jesuit Global Network of Schools, 388 JRS schools, 2,127 Fe y Alegría schools (3,629 institutions).

In the late 1960s control of several prominent Catholic universities passed from the founding religious orders to independent boards of trustees composed mainly of lay people, and this became the norm for nearly all US Catholic colleges through the 1970s.

The Monita Secreta, purported secret instructions of the Jesuits, appeared in Kraków in 1614/1615; its likely author was Jerome Zahorowski, expelled from the Society in 1613; many scholars and the British Museum regard it as an anti-Jesuit forgery/apocryphal.

vt8_opus_dei.topic: Opus Dei: founding, prelature, Francis's 2022 and 2023 changes, statutes, membership, criticism and its response

claims.text: Escrivá founded Opus Dei in Madrid on 2 October 1928; approved as a secular institute 1947 (provisional) and 1950; made a personal prelature by John Paul II's Ut sit (1982); Escrivá beatified 1992, canonized 2002; Fernando Ocáriz prelate since 23 January 2017.

Ut sit erecting the prelature is dated 28 November 1982. Ad charisma tuendum (14 July 2022, in force 4 August 2022): 'the Prelature depends on the Dicastery for the Clergy'; the prelate must report each year; 'the Prelate shall not be honoured with the episcopal order'; he receives the title Supernumerary Apostolic Protonotary.

Motu proprio in force 8 August 2023 amended canons 295–296: personal prelatures are 'similar to public clerical associations of pontifical law with the ability to incardinate clerics', the prelate is Moderator with an Ordinary's faculties, and 'the laity can dedicate themselves to the apostolic works of the personal prelature'.

Opus Dei states it has about 93,000 members (around 90,000 in summary), about 2,095 priests (2%), 98% laity, about 70% supernumeraries (mostly married); numeraries are celibate and usually live in Opus Dei centres.
Revised statutes were submitted to the Dicastery for the Clergy on 11 June 2025 after an Extraordinary General Congress in April 2023; Ocáriz: 'The Prelature awaits the Holy See's response.'
On 16 February 2026 Leo XIV told Ocáriz that the updating of the statutes 'continues in its study phase and that no publication date can yet be foreseen' (per a prelature statement).

Some members served as ministers under Franco (e.g. Alberto Ullastres); critics cite this as influence, while historians Paul Preston and Brian Crozier say they were chosen for talent; critics include former members María del Carmen Tapia and Vladimir Felzmann; a 2024 Financial Times/El País report alleged numerary assistants were 'coerced into domestic servitude'; Opus Dei denied it and called Gareth Gore's book 'a false picture … based on distorted facts, conspiracy theories and outright lies'; Opus Dei has no monks or nuns.

Argentina: 43 women (members 1974–2015) complained; after a two-year investigation with the trafficking prosecutor's office, prosecutors named four former regional vicars and on 11 June 2025 asked to question Mariano Fazio; no convictions; Opus Dei 'categorically denies' trafficking or labour exploitation.
Opus Dei's position (28 July 2025): it 'categorically rejects the accusation of trafficking and exploitation'; the judge has taken over; no one has been charged and no trial is underway.

As of 11 September 2026 Judge Daniel Rafecas (Federal Court No. 3) had not carried out any of the requested questionings (indagatorias) of Fazio and four former vicars (Nannei, Olmos, Urrestarazu, Dondo); Ending Clergy Abuse asked him to advance the case; it covers more than 40 women.

vt8_order_of_malta.topic: Sovereign Military Order of Malta: origins, sovereignty, relations, UN, Holy See link, 2016–17 crisis, 2022 charter, Malteser International

claims.text: Merchants of Amalfi obtained permission from the Caliph of Egypt in the second half of the 11th century to build a church, convent and hospital of St John in Jerusalem; under Blessed Gerard the community became a lay religious order; Paschal II's bull of 15 February 1113 recognised it, placed it under the Church's protection and gave it the right to elect its superiors; 81 Grand Masters from Gerard to Fra' John Dunlap.

Rhodes 1310–1523 (negotiated surrender after Suleiman's siege); Malta granted 1530 by Charles V and Joanna with Clement VII's approval under the tribute of the Maltese falcon; Napoleon took Malta in June 1798; seat in Rome from 1834; Italy recognises Palazzo Malta (Via Condotti 68) and the Villa del Priorato (Aventine) as extraterritorial; 1953 Tribunal of Cardinals called its sovereignty 'functional'; Italian Cassation 1974 treated it as a foreign state; Brownlie argues its capacity is limited; about 13,500 members, ~52,000 employees and ~95,000–100,000 volunteers; 1929 Italian decree: Grand Master enjoys 'the honors due to the Cardinals'; Dunlap elected 3 May 2023 for a ten-year term, renewable once, not beyond 85; Boeselager removed Dec 2016 after Malteser International-linked condom distribution in Myanmar; Festing resigned 24 Jan 2017; Becciu named special delegate 2 Feb 2017.

The Order states it has diplomatic relations with 118 countries, plus the EU, permanent observer status at the UN, cooperation agreements with over 50 states, and accredited missions in more than 100 countries (page modified 29 September 2026).

Wikipedia's list: relations with 114 UN members and the Holy See (elsewhere '115 sovereign states including the Holy See'); latest entry Andorra 16 June 2025; Holy See relations dated February 1930; EU 1987; ambassadors exchanged with the State of Palestine.
UNGA resolution 48/265 of 24 August 1994, adopted without a vote, invited the Sovereign Military Order of Malta to participate in the sessions and work of the General Assembly as an observer.

Boeselager dismissed as Grand Chancellor in December 2016; on 22 December 2016 the Holy See formed a group to investigate; on 10 January 2017 the Order called the dismissal 'an internal act of governance' and the group 'legally irrelevant' given its sovereignty; on 24 January 2017 Francis asked Festing to resign; the resignation was accepted 25 January.

Francis's decree of 3 September 2022 promulgated the new Constitutional Charter and Melitense Code with immediate effect, revoked the High Offices, dissolved the Sovereign Council, appointed a provisional Council and convened an Extraordinary General Chapter for 25 January 2023; it quotes the 1953 judgment that the Order is 'a religious Order, approved by the Holy See' and states 'being a religious Order, it depends … on the Holy See'.

The Order's statement of 3 September 2022: Charter and Code 'enter into force today'; provisional Sovereign Council members (Dunlap as Lieutenant, Rousseau, Paternò di Montecupo, de Franciscis, Fabrizio Colonna) took the oath.
On 16 October 2012 the Holy See said it 'recognizes and protects only the Sovereign Military Order of Malta' and the Equestrian Order of the Holy Sepulchre, besides its own five pontifical orders.

Malteser International 2024: 152 projects in 36 countries; 7.2 million people supported (3.2 million emergency relief); 1,202 staff; programme spending about €74.5m; revenue €105.8m; Middle East and North Africa €30.7m across 18 projects in 6 countries; 200 tons of food to Gaza; a container clinic in Gaza prepared with the Latin Patriarchate; Holy Family Hospital Bethlehem a focus; Lebanon: 7 mobile units and 11 health centres.
